title: The first sight: an old man
hook: on a chariot ride with Channa he sees a man bent with age and asks, will this happen to me
carry: this is coming for all of us
tomorrow: the second sight: a sick man

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasodhara: in the stories she is the prince's equal, and one day a nun in her own right. Your line was partner, not prize. Who did you honor as an equal? Day thirty-one.

The oldest face you know well. A grandmother, a neighbor, the man who has run the corner shop since before you were born. Now take it away: a whole childhood without one face like that. Not once. The stories say the young prince grew up exactly that way. His father, remembering the prophecy that his son might leave and become a teacher, kept every sad thing out of sight. Three palaces, music, gardens, young and beautiful people everywhere. Then one day the prince asks his charioteer, Channa, to drive him out to the park. The road has been swept and decorated. And still, at the side of it, there stands a man. Today, the first of four things the prince was never meant to see.
screen: `THE OLDEST FACE YOU KNOW.` → `A PALACE WITH NO OLD FACES.` → `A MAN BY THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The man is bent almost double. Gray hair, few teeth, leaning on a stick, trembling as he walks. The prince has never seen anything like him. What is wrong with that man, he asks. His hair isn't like other people's hair. His body isn't like other bodies. Channa answers plainly: that is what we call an old man. And the prince asks the question the whole story turns on. Will this happen to me? Channa doesn't soften it. Yes. To you, to me, to everyone. Nobody gets past old age. The prince tells him to turn the chariot around. No park today. He goes home and sits alone with it. There's a wrinkle in the sources. In the Pali discourses, this story of the four sights is told about a Buddha from long ago, named Vipassi. Later biographies tell it about Siddhattha, and that's the version told in temples and picture books today. And remember the Buddha's own, quieter memory from the three palaces: the pride of youth falling away. Either way, the point is the same. The prince didn't learn a new fact. Everyone knows people grow old. What changed is that he let it mean him. Old age stopped being something that happens to other people. That shift, from them to me, is where Buddhists say the path begins to open.
screen: `WHAT IS WRONG WITH THAT MAN?` · `WILL THIS HAPPEN TO ME?` · `A STORY TOLD OF AN OLDER BUDDHA.` · `FROM THEM TO ME.` · then, large: `THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one old face you know. Look at it slowly, the way the prince looked from the chariot. The lines around the eyes. The hands. Now let a quiet thought arrive: this face was once young, like mine. And my face is on its way to being old, like this one. Don't turn it into fear. Just let the two faces sit side by side, kindly. If there is gratitude for this person, let it come. The bell holds the time.
Channa. The prince's charioteer, who drove him past an old man and couldn't soften the truth: this will happen to you too. The first of four sights that turned his life around.
Your line: this is coming for all of us. Today, look kindly at one old face, in a shop, on a bus, in a photo, and let it be a face you're on your way to. Day thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 31 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SECOND SIGHT: A SICK MAN.`

howItsDone: Buddhists retell the four sights as the beginning of the Buddha's search, and one's own aging is the first of the five remembrances, which the Buddha said should be reflected on often.

fork.setup: you're the prince. your charioteer has just told you that you, too, will grow old. what do you do?
options: carry on to the park and forget it.
turn the chariot around and go home to think.
order the old man taken off the road.
fork.reveal: he turns back. no park today. the story says he went home and sat with it, and the palace's music couldn't reach him.

original.note: Pali: old age, aging. The first of the sights, and the first of the five remembrances.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince had never seen an old person, which seems impossible.
what it means: the story is about the moment old age stops being about other people and starts being about you.
what a scholar hears: the four sights appear in the Mahapadana Sutta (DN 14) about the past Buddha Vipassi; the commentaries and later biographies transfer the story to Siddhattha.

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the four sights, told of the Buddha Vipassi
Sukhumala Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 3.38): the Buddha remembers the pride of youth falling away
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the first sight on the road to the park

notes: The four sights: in the canon (DN 14) the story is told of Vipassi; the Nidanakatha and Buddhacarita tell it of Siddhattha. Confirm this framing is appropriate for the path.
In the Nidanakatha the gods place the old man on the road; that detail is left out here. A Keeper may want it in.
AN 3.38 paraphrased: the Buddha reflects that people are repelled by the old, forgetting they will age, and the intoxication of youth leaves him. Confirm wording.
Channa's answer that 'nobody gets past old age' follows DN 14's charioteer (all are subject to aging); confirm.

Editor review (days 20-37 pass): hook no longer opens 'Think of'; cut the stock 'here's something most people never hear', the 'written centuries after' date claim and 'the whole Buddhist world'; the AN 3.38 pride-of-youth passage was retold in full two days after day 29 taught it, so it is now a one-line callback; 'daily' and 'many monasteries' removed from the five remembrances (AN 5.57 says 'often').
